prompt: Molecular orbital theory is described as a conceptual extension of which model?

choices.text: The orbital model of atomic structure
The Bohr model of circular electron orbits
choices.why: Bohr's orbits were replaced by quantum mechanics. MO theory extends the orbital model, so successful for atoms, to molecules.

choices.text: The classical model of a vibrating string
choices.why: That was the classical wave equation. MO theory extends the atomic orbital model: a molecule is treated like an atom with more nuclei.

choices.text: The Lewis model of shared electron pairs
choices.why: H_2^+ is bonded by a single electron, not a pair. MO theory is an extension of the orbital model used for atoms.

explanation: Molecular orbital theory extends the orbital model that worked so well for atoms. As was once playfully remarked, a molecule is nothing more than an atom with more nuclei.

prompt: Why does the study of diatomic molecules begin with H_2^+?

choices.text: Like the H atom, it is exactly solvable
It is the most common molecule in the universe
choices.why: H_2^+ has only a transient existence. It comes first because it is the simplest molecule and can be solved exactly, as the hydrogen atom could.

choices.text: It is the only molecule with two electrons
choices.why: H_2^+ has one electron, not two. It comes first because, like the hydrogen atom, it is a prototype that can be solved exactly.

choices.text: Its bond can be explained without quantum mechanics
choices.why: Its electron still needs the Schrödinger equation. H_2^+ comes first because that equation can be solved exactly for it, as for the hydrogen atom.

explanation: Our understanding of atomic orbitals began with the exactly solvable hydrogen atom. Molecular orbital theory likewise starts from another exactly solvable prototype, the hydrogen molecular ion H_2^+.

prompt: What particles make up H_2^+, the simplest conceivable molecule?

choices.text: Two protons and one electron
Two protons and two electrons
choices.why: That is the neutral H2 molecule. Removing one electron leaves H_2^+: two protons held together by a single electron.

choices.text: One proton and one electron
choices.why: That is a hydrogen atom, with only one nucleus. A molecule needs at least two nuclei; H_2^+ has two protons and one electron.

choices.text: One proton and two electrons
choices.why: That is the hydride ion, H^−, with one nucleus. H_2^+ has two protons and one electron, giving a charge of +1.

explanation: The simplest conceivable molecule has two protons and one electron: H_2^+, the hydrogen molecular ion. Its overall charge is +2 − 1 = +1.

prompt: Where has H_2^+ actually been found?

choices.text: Briefly, in electric discharges in hydrogen gas
As a stable gas that can be stored in cylinders
choices.why: H_2^+ has only a transient existence. It forms in electrical discharges through hydrogen gas and has been seen by mass spectrometry and in outer space.

choices.text: Nowhere; it is known only from calculations on paper
choices.why: It has been detected by mass spectrometry and in outer space, and it forms briefly in electrical discharges through hydrogen gas.

choices.text: In solid ionic crystals, paired with negative ions
choices.why: It isn't found in stable salts. It forms briefly in electrical discharges through hydrogen gas and has also been detected in outer space.

explanation: H_2^+ has a transient existence in electrical discharges through hydrogen gas. It has been detected by mass spectrometry and also in outer space.

prompt: In what sense can the Schrödinger equation for H_2^+ be solved exactly?

choices.text: Exactly, as long as the nuclei are held fixed
Exactly, including the motion of the nuclei
choices.why: The exact solution treats the protons as fixed, within the Born-Oppenheimer approximation. Nuclear motion is handled separately.

choices.text: Only by the variational method, never exactly
choices.why: With fixed nuclei it can be solved exactly, because there is only one electron. The section still develops approximate LCAO solutions for use with other molecules.

choices.text: Exactly, because the two protons don't repel
choices.why: The protons do repel; that is the e^2/(4πε_0 R) term. The equation can be solved exactly within the Born-Oppenheimer approximation, with the nuclei fixed.

explanation: With the nuclei fixed (the Born-Oppenheimer approximation), the one-electron Schrödinger equation for H_2^+ can be solved exactly. The motion of the nuclei is not part of that exact solution.

prompt: The Schrödinger equation for H_2^+ can be solved exactly. Why does the section develop approximate solutions for it instead?

choices.text: To reuse the method for molecules with more electrons
Because the exact solution gives the wrong energy
choices.why: Within the Born-Oppenheimer approximation the exact solution really is exact. Approximate methods are developed so they can be used for diatomic molecules with more than one electron.

choices.text: Because H_2^+ has never been observed in nature
choices.why: It has been observed, in electrical discharges and in outer space. Approximations are used so the method carries over to molecules with more than one electron.

choices.text: Because approximate solutions are always more accurate
choices.why: Nothing is more accurate than an exact solution. The approximate method is chosen because it carries over to diatomic molecules with more electrons.

explanation: Because there is only one electron, H_2^+ can be solved exactly. The section develops approximate solutions in a way that also applies to diatomic molecules with more than one electron, which can't be solved exactly.

prompt: The two protons in H_2^+ repel each other. What holds them together?

choices.text: Their attraction to the single electron
The strong nuclear force between the protons
choices.why: The section explains the bond with electrostatic forces only. The electron's negative charge between the protons attracts both of them.

choices.text: A magnetic attraction between the two protons
choices.why: The forces involved are electrostatic. The single electron's negative charge, placed between the protons, attracts both and counteracts their repulsion.

choices.text: A second electron shared between the protons
choices.why: H_2^+ has only one electron. That single electron, with its charge density between the protons, holds them together.

explanation: H_2^+ is two protons held together by the electrostatic force of a single electron. The electron's attraction to both protons counteracts their Coulomb repulsion.

prompt: Where must the electron's negative charge density be high for it to pull the two protons of H_2^+ together?

choices.text: In the region between the two protons
On the far side of each proton, away from the other
choices.why: Charge there would pull each proton outward, away from the other. Negative charge between the protons pulls both inward.

choices.text: Spread evenly over all space around the ion
choices.why: An even spread doesn't favor the space between the nuclei. A high density between the protons is what pulls them together.

choices.text: Exactly at the position of one of the protons
choices.why: Charge sitting on one proton doesn't pull the two together. A high negative charge density between them does.

explanation: To create a chemical bond between two positively charged nuclei, a high density of negative charge between them is needed. The molecular orbitals of H_2^+ should reflect this.

prompt: In the electronic Hamiltonian for H_2^+, what are r_A and r_B?

choices.text: The electron's distances from protons A and B
The sizes (radii) of protons A and B themselves
choices.why: Proton size plays no part. r_A and r_B are the distances of the electron from protons A and B.

choices.text: The distances of the protons from the midpoint
choices.why: Each of those would be R/2 and fixed. r_A and r_B change as the electron moves: they are its distances from protons A and B.

choices.text: The distance between protons A and B
choices.why: That is R. r_A and r_B are the distances from the electron to proton A and to proton B.

explanation: r_A and r_B are the distances of the electron from protons A and B, and R is the distance between the protons. The terms −e^2/(4πε_0 r_A) and −e^2/(4πε_0 r_B) are the electron's attraction to each proton.

prompt: In H_2^+ the protons are R = 106 pm apart. The electron is on the straight line between them, r_A = 30 pm from proton A. How far is it from proton B, r_B, in pm?
explanation: On the line between the protons, r_A + r_B = R, so r_B = 106 pm − 30 pm = 76 pm. As the electron moves, r_A and r_B change, but R stays fixed.

prompt: In the kinetic energy term −(ħ^2/(2m))∇^2 of the H_2^+ electronic Hamiltonian, whose mass is m?

choices.text: The electron's mass
The mass of one proton
choices.why: With the protons held fixed, they have no kinetic energy term. The only kinetic energy is the electron's, so m is the electron mass.

choices.text: The total mass of the H_2^+ ion
choices.why: The term describes the electron's motion only; the motion of the whole ion isn't included. m is the electron mass.

choices.text: The reduced mass of the two protons
choices.why: A reduced mass of the protons would describe their vibration, which isn't in the electronic Hamiltonian. m is the mass of the electron.

explanation: The electronic Hamiltonian has only one kinetic energy term, for the single electron, so m is the electron mass. The protons are held fixed, so they contribute no kinetic energy.

prompt: With the two protons held fixed, which term of the H_2^+ electronic Hamiltonian has the same value wherever the electron is?

choices.text: +e^2/(4πε_0 R), the proton–proton repulsion
−e^2/(4πε_0 r_A), the attraction to proton A
choices.why: r_A changes as the electron moves, so this term does too. Only the term with R, the fixed distance between the protons, stays the same.

choices.text: −(ħ^2/(2m))∇^2, the electron's kinetic energy
choices.why: This operator acts on the electron's wavefunction and depends on how it varies in space. The constant term is the proton–proton repulsion, which depends only on R.

choices.text: None; every term changes as the electron moves
choices.why: The proton–proton term doesn't involve the electron at all. With the nuclei fixed, e^2/(4πε_0 R) is just a number.

explanation: R is the distance between the two protons. With the nuclei fixed, +e^2/(4πε_0 R), their Coulomb repulsion, is just a number, while the other terms depend on where the electron is.

prompt: In the H_2^+ Hamiltonian, the terms with r_A and r_B are negative, but the term with R is positive. Why?

choices.text: Attraction lowers the energy; repulsion raises it
Repulsion lowers the energy; attraction raises it
choices.why: It's the reverse: opposite charges attracting lowers the energy (negative terms), and like charges repelling raises it (positive term).

choices.text: The distances r_A and r_B are negative numbers
choices.why: Distances are always positive. The minus signs show the attraction between the electron and each proton, which lowers the energy.

choices.text: The electron has more charge than a proton
choices.why: The electron and proton have charges of the same size, −e and +e. The signs come from attraction (negative) versus repulsion (positive).

explanation: The electron and each proton have opposite charges and attract, which lowers the energy: −e^2/(4πε_0 r_A) and −e^2/(4πε_0 r_B). The two protons have like charges and repel, which raises it: +e^2/(4πε_0 R).

prompt: Put the electron of H_2^+ at the midpoint between the protons, so r_A = R/2. How many times larger is its attraction to proton A, e^2/(4πε_0 r_A), than the proton–proton repulsion, e^2/(4πε_0 R)?
explanation: With r_A = R/2, e^2/(4πε_0 r_A) = 2e^2/(4πε_0 R), twice the repulsion. Counting proton B as well, the attraction is four times the repulsion: negative charge between the protons can hold them together.

prompt: Compared with the electronic Hamiltonian of a hydrogen atom, which terms are new in the Hamiltonian for H_2^+?

choices.text: An attraction to proton B and a proton–proton repulsion
An electron–electron repulsion and a second kinetic energy
choices.why: H_2^+ still has only one electron, so neither term appears. What's new is the second proton: the electron's attraction to it and its repulsion with proton A.

choices.text: Kinetic energy terms for proton A and for proton B
choices.why: The nuclei are fixed in the electronic Hamiltonian, so there is no nuclear kinetic energy. The new terms are the attraction to proton B and the proton–proton repulsion.

choices.text: An attraction to proton B and an electron–electron repulsion
choices.why: The attraction to proton B is new, but with one electron there is no electron–electron repulsion. The other new term is the repulsion between the protons.

explanation: A hydrogen atom's Hamiltonian has the electron's kinetic energy and its attraction to one proton. H_2^+ adds the attraction −e^2/(4πε_0 r_B) to the second proton and the repulsion +e^2/(4πε_0 R) between the two protons.

prompt: Why does the electronic Hamiltonian for H_2^+ have no electron–electron repulsion term?

choices.text: H_2^+ has only one electron
The Born-Oppenheimer approximation drops that term
choices.why: The approximation drops the nuclear kinetic energy, not electron repulsion. There's no such term because H_2^+ has a single electron.

choices.text: Its two electrons are too far apart to repel
choices.why: H_2^+ doesn't have two electrons. With only one electron there is nothing for it to repel.

choices.text: The protons cancel out the electron repulsion
choices.why: Protons attract electrons; they don't cancel repulsion between them. H_2^+ simply has one electron, so no repulsion term is needed.

explanation: With only one electron, there is no electron–electron repulsion. This is why H_2^+, like the hydrogen atom, can be solved exactly once the nuclei are fixed.

prompt: If the two protons of H_2^+ are pulled infinitely far apart, what is left?

choices.text: A hydrogen atom and an isolated proton
Two hydrogen atoms, each with one electron
choices.why: There is only one electron to go around. Pulled apart, it stays with one proton as a hydrogen atom; the other proton is bare.

choices.text: Two protons, each with half an electron
choices.why: An electron can't be split in half. It ends up near one proton (a hydrogen atom), leaving the other proton isolated.

choices.text: Two bare protons and a free electron
choices.why: Separating the protons doesn't remove the electron. It stays bound to one of them as a hydrogen atom.

explanation: When the protons are infinitely far apart, the electron is near one proton or the other, giving a hydrogen atom and an isolated proton. The electronic wavefunction is then 1s_A or 1s_B.

prompt: In the LCAO treatment of H_2^+, what does 1s_A denote?

choices.text: A hydrogen 1s orbital centered on proton A
A 1s orbital centered midway between A and B
choices.why: 1s_A uses proton A as the origin of its coordinates. A 1s orbital centered on proton B is 1s_B.

choices.text: The molecular orbital of H_2^+ near proton A
choices.why: 1s_A is an atomic orbital, one of the basis functions. The molecular orbital is built by combining 1s_A and 1s_B.

choices.text: An excited state of the electron on proton A
choices.why: 1s is the lowest hydrogen orbital, not an excited one. 1s_A is the hydrogen 1s orbital with proton A as its origin.

explanation: 1s_A is a hydrogen 1s atomic orbital with proton A as the origin of the spherical polar coordinates that locate the electron. Similarly, 1s_B has proton B as its origin.

prompt: Why is a combination of 1s_A and 1s_B a sensible starting guess for the molecular orbital of H_2^+?

choices.text: Far apart, the electron's orbital is 1s_A or 1s_B
1s_A and 1s_B are exact solutions for H_2^+
choices.why: They are exact for a hydrogen atom, not for H_2^+. They're a good start because the electron is in one of them when the protons are far apart.

choices.text: The electron always stays midway between the protons
choices.why: The electron isn't confined to the midpoint. The combination works because, with the protons far apart, the electron is in 1s_A or 1s_B.

choices.text: Any two functions would work equally well
choices.why: The choice matters. Hydrogen 1s orbitals are natural because they describe the electron exactly when it is near only one of the two protons.

explanation: With the protons infinitely far apart, the electron is in 1s_A or 1s_B, depending on which proton it is near. So when the protons are close, a useful approximation is a linear combination of these two atomic orbitals.

prompt: Which expression is the LCAO molecular orbital that the section uses for H_2^+?

choices.text: ψ = C_A 1s_A + C_B 1s_B
ψ = C × 1s_A × 1s_B
choices.why: LCAO combines atomic orbitals by adding them with coefficients, not by multiplying them. The MO is C_A 1s_A + C_B 1s_B.

choices.text: ψ = C_A 1s_A + C_A 2s_A
choices.why: Both of these orbitals sit on proton A. The H_2^+ MO combines a 1s orbital on each proton: C_A 1s_A + C_B 1s_B.

choices.text: ψ = 1s_A, with no 1s_B part
choices.why: That describes the electron near A only, as when the protons are far apart. When they are close, the MO combines both: C_A 1s_A + C_B 1s_B.

explanation: The LCAO-MO method writes the molecular orbital as a linear combination of atomic orbitals, ψ(r) = C_A 1s_A(r) + C_B 1s_B(r). The two basis functions are the hydrogen 1s orbitals on protons A and B.

prompt: The number of molecular orbitals from an LCAO calculation equals the number of atomic orbitals in the expansion. Suppose the expansion for H_2^+ used the 1s, the 2s and all three 2p orbitals on each proton. How many molecular orbitals would it give?
explanation: Each proton contributes 1 + 1 + 3 = 5 atomic orbitals, so there are 2 × 5 = 10 in all, giving 10 molecular orbitals. The section's own expansion, with just 1s_A and 1s_B, gives two.

prompt: In ψ = C_A 1s_A + C_B 1s_B for H_2^+, what does |C_A|^2 give?

choices.text: The probability that the electron is near proton A
The probability that the electron is near proton B
choices.why: That is |C_B|^2. |C_A|^2 goes with the orbital centered on proton A.

choices.text: The energy of the electron in the 1s_A orbital
choices.why: Coefficients don't give energies. |C_A|^2 is the probability that the electron is near proton A.

choices.text: The distance of the electron from proton A
choices.why: That distance is r_A, a coordinate, not a coefficient. |C_A|^2 is the probability that the electron is near proton A.

explanation: The probabilities that the electron is near A and near B are |C_A|^2 and |C_B|^2. For the two identical protons of H_2^+ they must be equal.

prompt: Which two choices of the coefficients both satisfy |C_A|^2 = |C_B|^2 for H_2^+?

choices.text: C_A = C_B and C_A = −C_B
C_A = 2C_B and C_B = 2C_A
choices.why: These make one probability four times the other. Equal probabilities need C_A = ±C_B.

choices.text: C_A = 1, C_B = 0 and C_A = 0, C_B = 1
choices.why: Each puts the electron entirely on one proton, so |C_A|^2 ≠ |C_B|^2. The two choices are C_A = C_B and C_A = −C_B.

choices.text: C_A = C_B = 0 and C_A = C_B = 1
choices.why: Zero coefficients give no orbital at all. The two choices are C_A = C_B, giving ψ_(+), and C_A = −C_B, giving ψ_(−).

explanation: Two possibilities satisfy |C_A|^2 = |C_B|^2: C_A = C_B = C_(+) and C_A = −C_B = C_(−). They give the two molecular orbitals ψ_(+) = C_(+)(1s_A + 1s_B) and ψ_(−) = C_(−)(1s_A − 1s_B).

prompt: For the H_2^+ molecular orbital with C_A = −C_B, the coefficient C_A is 0.55. What is C_B?
explanation: C_B = −C_A = −0.55. Then |C_A|^2 = |C_B|^2 = 0.3025, so the electron is equally likely to be near either proton, as it must be for two identical protons.

prompt: What do the labels + and − in ψ_(+) and ψ_(−) refer to?

choices.text: Whether 1s_A and 1s_B are added or subtracted
The charges of the protons and of the electron
choices.why: The labels have nothing to do with charge. ψ_(+) is the sum 1s_A + 1s_B and ψ_(−) is the difference 1s_A − 1s_B.

choices.text: The spin of the electron, up or down
choices.why: Spin isn't part of these spatial orbitals. The + and − show whether the two 1s orbitals are added or subtracted.

choices.text: Whether the orbital energy is positive or negative
choices.why: The labels come from the combination, not from the sign of the energy: ψ_(+) = C_(+)(1s_A + 1s_B) and ψ_(−) = C_(−)(1s_A − 1s_B).

explanation: ψ_(+) = C_(+)(1s_A + 1s_B) comes from C_A = C_B, and ψ_(−) = C_(−)(1s_A − 1s_B) from C_A = −C_B. The labels record whether the two atomic orbitals are added or subtracted.

prompt: How does the electron charge density of ψ_(+) = C_(+)(1s_A + 1s_B) compare with that of ψ_(−) = C_(−)(1s_A − 1s_B)?

choices.text: ψ_(+) has more density between the two protons
ψ_(+) has less density between the two protons
choices.why: It's ψ_(−) whose density is diminished between the protons, with a node in the middle. ψ_(+) enhances the density there.

choices.text: ψ_(+) has a node midway between the protons
choices.why: The node is in ψ_(−), where 1s_A and 1s_B cancel. In ψ_(+) they add, building up density between the protons.

choices.text: ψ_(+) puts all its density on proton A
choices.why: |C_A|^2 = |C_B|^2, so both protons share the density equally. What sets ψ_(+) apart is the extra density between them.

explanation: In ψ_(+) the two 1s orbitals add, so the charge density is enhanced between the protons, as our intuitive picture of a bond requires. In ψ_(−) they subtract: the density between the protons is diminished, with a node in the middle.

prompt: The section says the electron wavefunction oscillates according to the Schrödinger wave equation. What does it say orbitals are?

choices.text: The standing waves of the electron wavefunction
The circular paths along which the electron travels
choices.why: Orbitals aren't paths; that is the old idea of orbits. The section calls orbitals the standing waves of the electron wavefunction.

choices.text: Traveling waves that carry the electron between atoms
choices.why: Orbitals don't travel from place to place. They are standing waves of the electron wavefunction, like the modes of a string fixed at both ends.

choices.text: Regions where the wavefunction is exactly zero
choices.why: Those are nodes, places within an orbital where ψ = 0. The orbitals themselves are the standing waves of the electron wavefunction.

explanation: The electron wavefunction oscillates according to the Schrödinger wave equation, and orbitals are its standing waves. The bonding and antibonding orbitals of H_2^+ are standing waves too, built from the 1s waves on the two protons.
